short: Zhou authority dissolved into competing states, and Confucius taught in the wreckage.
full:
The period takes its name from the Spring and Autumn Annals, the terse year-by-year chronicle kept by the state of Lu between 722 and 481 BCE. It opens with the Zhou court's flight east in 770 BCE, after which real power lay with the regional lords. Well over a hundred polities are named in the sources; by its close a handful had swallowed the rest. Rather than depose the king, the strongest ruler of the day took the title of hegemon and convened the others in his name, beginning with Duke Huan of Qi in 679 BCE.

Iron tools spread, ox-drawn ploughing extended cultivation, and warfare shifted from chariot duels between aristocrats towards mass infantry levies. The political disorder produced the most consequential intellectual movement in Chinese history. Confucius, born in Lu in 551 BCE, spent his life arguing that ritual propriety and the cultivation of character, not force, held a society together. His followers, and the rival schools that answered him, framed Chinese political thought for the next two millennia.
